## Status and conclusion

This is a deliberately local working note. It temporarily lives with experiment
77 so that the method used there and its literature can be read together. It
should eventually be consolidated into the research notes or a paper methods
section.

The short conclusion is:

> With fixed casewise contributions, multiplying every contribution by an
> independent Rademacher variable is algebraically identical to sign flipping
> it. Thus experiment 77's retained Rademacher comparator is both a
> sign-flipped-score procedure and a multiplier score bootstrap. The substantial
> differences lie in the inferential framework: the allowed weight laws, the
> construction of the reference distribution, centering and studentization,
> and whether validity comes from finite-sample group invariance or only from a
> conditional central limit theorem.

Experiment 77 now uses **Mammen multiplier calibration of an
observed-sensitivity nuisance-effective global score test** as its primary FIML
procedure. The former expected-information Rademacher construction is retained
as a comparator. Only that comparator is algebraically a sign flip. Neither
construction is an exact finite-sample randomization test under nonnormal FIML
data.

## What experiment 77 computes

Let the saturated moment parameter be

$$
\eta=
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{vech}(\Sigma)\\
\mu
\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^m,
$$

with the mean block omitted for covariance-only complete-data models. At the
restricted SEM estimate $\widehat\theta$, let $s_i$ be case $i$'s score with
respect to $\eta$. For FIML, $s_i$ is the observed-data score for that case's
missingness pattern; missing entries are never filled in.

Let

$$
\Delta=\frac{\partial\eta(\theta)}{\partial\theta^{\mathsf T}}
$$

be the local SEM tangent, after incorporating affine equality constraints. Let
$K$ be an orthonormal basis for $\operatorname{col}(\Delta)$ and $D$ an
orthonormal basis for its Euclidean complement. If $A$ is the realized
observed-data saturated-moment sensitivity, define

$$
G_A
=D-K(K^{\mathsf T}AK)^{-1}K^{\mathsf T}AD.
$$

The construction ensures

$$
K^{\mathsf T}AG_A=0.
$$

Thus the columns of $G_A$ represent saturated directions made orthogonal, in
the sensitivity metric, to changes locally explained by the fitted SEM. The
casewise effective contributions and their sum are

$$
z_i=G_A^{\mathsf T}s_i,
\qquad
u=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i.
$$

With

$$
V=G_A^{\mathsf T}IG_A,
$$

the observed statistic is

$$
T=u^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}u.
$$

Here $I$ and $V$ are sample-summed quantities. Equivalently, one may divide
$u$ by $\sqrt n$ and $V$ by $n$; the quadratic statistic is unchanged. The
dimension

$$
d=m-\operatorname{rank}(\Delta)
$$

is ordinarily the SEM model degrees of freedom.

For draw $b$, the primary FIML procedure generates independent Mammen
multipliers $w_{ib}$ with mean zero, variance one, and third moment one, and
computes

$$
u_b=\sum_{i=1}^n w_{ib}z_i,
\qquad
T_b=u_b^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}u_b.
$$

With $B$ random draws, the reported Monte Carlo p-value is

$$
\widehat p
=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^B\mathbf 1(T_b\geq T)}{B+1}.
$$

Here $I$ is the positive-definite pattern-conditional Gaussian Fisher metric.
The nuisance sensitivity $A$ and the common quadratic metric have distinct
roles. Multiplier validity requires the first-order effective rows to use $A$
and permits any fixed positive-definite limiting quadratic. The fitted moments,
tangent projection, and metric $V$ remain fixed. No
saturated model and no bootstrap SEM is fitted. Experiment 77 uses $B=199$, so
the p-value grid has width $1/200$. The legacy comparator substitutes the
pattern-conditional Fisher information $I$ for $A$ and uses Rademacher
multipliers.

## Why the nuisance projection appears

The construction is the classical effective-score correction in a different
coordinate system. Partition a parameter into tested and nuisance components,
$(\beta,\gamma)$, with casewise scores
$\psi_{\beta i}$ and $\psi_{\gamma i}$. Let $A$ be the sensitivity, or
negative expected derivative of the score, partitioned conformably. Under the
null,

$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\gamma-\gamma_0)
=A_{\gamma\gamma}^{-1}
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{\gamma i}+o_p(1).
$$

Expanding the tested score around $\gamma_0$ gives

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi_{\beta i}(\widehat\gamma)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(
\psi_{\beta i}
-A_{\beta\gamma}A_{\gamma\gamma}^{-1}\psi_{\gamma i}
\right)
+o_p(1).
$$

The expression in parentheses is the nuisance-effective score contribution.
It is the score-test/C(alpha) construction of @neyman1959 and the effective
score developed pedagogically by @hall_mathiason1990. In experiment 77, the
tested coordinates are the saturated directions $D$, the nuisance coordinates
are the SEM tangent $K$, and the observed-data Hessian supplies the sensitivity
blocks. The matrix $G_A$ is exactly the coordinate-free version of the
subtraction above.

This correction matters for resampling. At a restricted optimum the **sum** of
the nuisance score is zero, so using the raw tested score or the effective score
can give the same observed statistic. Their individual rows differ, however.
Multipliers act on the individual rows, and only the effective rows reproduce
the first-order effect of estimating the nuisance parameter. This is the main
point of the effective sign-flip construction in
@hemerik_goeman_finos2020.

## What the multiplier distribution approximates

Write the normalized effective score as

$$
U_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n z_i.
$$

Suppose, under the null, that the rows are independent, have mean zero, satisfy
a Lindeberg condition, and have limiting average covariance

$$
B_z=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\operatorname{Var}(z_i).
$$

Then

$$
U_n\Rightarrow N(0,B_z).
$$

Conditionally on the observed rows, multipliers with
$E(\xi_i)=0$ and $E(\xi_i^2)=1$ give

$$
U_n^*=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i z_i,
$$

with

$$
E_*(U_n^*)=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_*(U_n^*)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n z_i z_i^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Under the corresponding multiplier central limit theorem, the conditional law
of $U_n^*$ approaches the null law of $U_n$. General weighted-bootstrap theory
is developed by @praestgaard_wellner1993; direct resampling of estimating-
function summands appears in @hu_zidek1995 and @hu_kalbfleisch2000; and
@kline_santos2012 explicitly develops score perturbation for M-estimator Wald,
LM, and moment-restriction tests.

If the working metric $V/n$ converges to $V_0$, but $V_0\neq B_z$, then

$$
T\Rightarrow
Z^{\mathsf T}V_0^{-1}Z,
\qquad Z\sim N(0,B_z),
$$

which is generally a weighted sum of independent $\chi_1^2$ variables. The
multiplier draws reproduce this spectrum implicitly because their conditional
covariance estimates $B_z$. They do not need to form the full fourth-moment
matrix $B_z$ and diagonalize $V_0^{-1}B_z$. This connects the score multiplier
to the weighted-chi-square SEM asymptotics of @shapiro1983 and @satorra1989.

The often-used phrase "flipping kills the mean but preserves the covariance"
needs this conditional interpretation. The weights have conditional mean zero,
and their unit second moment preserves the empirical second moment of the fixed
rows. Sign flipping does not literally transform a nonzero-mean population into
the null population.

## Is sign flipping different from multiplier bootstrap?

### Algebraically: no, for Rademacher weights

For fixed rows $z_1,\ldots,z_n$,

$$
\xi_i z_i=
\begin{cases}
 z_i,&\xi_i=+1,\\
-z_i,&\xi_i=-1.
\end{cases}
$$

Consequently, a Rademacher multiplier draw and an independent sign-flip draw
produce exactly the same $u_b$ and $T_b$. There is no numerical or statistical
difference hiding behind the two names when the same rows, metric, and p-value
rule are used.

### Inferentially: sometimes

| Feature | Sign-randomization framing | Multiplier-bootstrap framing |
|---|---|---|
| Transformations | Usually the finite group $\{-1,+1\}^n$ | Independent mean-zero, unit-variance weights |
| Weight laws | Rademacher | Rademacher, Gaussian, Mammen, centered exponential, and others |
| Exactness route | Joint distribution invariant under all sign changes | None in general; conditional weak convergence |
| Asymptotic route | Approximate symmetry of a limiting statistic | Conditional multiplier CLT for an empirical/score process |
| Observed sample | Identity sign vector is one transformation in the rank | Observed statistic is compared with conditional bootstrap draws |
| Nuisance fitting | Can break sign invariance; effective scores repair first order | Influence-function/effective-score linearization repairs first order |
| Studentization | Optional; Hemerik et al. allow a common quadratic metric | Often explicit bootstrap-t or weighted-meat studentization |
| Non-Rademacher weights | No finite sign group or sign interpretation | Natural and sometimes chosen for higher-order moment matching |

If the joint null law of $(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ is invariant under arbitrary
componentwise sign changes, enumerating the sign group yields a finite-sample
randomization test. Randomly sampling group elements while retaining the
identity transformation yields a Monte Carlo version of that rank test. This
is a stronger conclusion than bootstrap consistency.

Mean-zero scores need not be symmetric. Under skewness, heteroskedasticity, or
estimated nuisance parameters, the required finite-sample group invariance will
usually fail. A sign-flip procedure can nevertheless be asymptotically valid
because the normalized score has a symmetric Gaussian limit. That is the
approximate-symmetry distinction formalized more generally by
@canay_romano_shaikh2017 and used for score contributions by
@hemerik_goeman_finos2020.

Conversely, Gaussian or Mammen weights may satisfy a multiplier theorem without
defining any transformation group of the observed data. Such procedures are
multiplier bootstraps, not sign-randomization tests. Mammen's asymmetric
two-point law is motivated by matching an additional weight moment and improving
higher-order behavior in regression settings [@mammen1993], building on the
wild-bootstrap line of @wu1986 and @liu1988.

Thus:

$$
\text{Rademacher sign flip}
\subset
\text{multiplier bootstrap algorithms},
$$

but a sign-randomization **validity theorem** and a multiplier-bootstrap
**validity theorem** do not have identical assumptions or conclusions.

## Centering and studentization

These two choices often account for apparent differences between implementations
that all say "multiplier score test."

### Centering

A conventional multiplier empirical process uses centered rows,

$$
\widetilde z_i=z_i-\bar z,
\qquad
\bar z=n^{-1}\sum_i z_i,
$$

whereas the basic sign-flip construction commonly multiplies the raw effective
rows. Under a correctly imposed null, $\bar z=O_p(n^{-1/2})$, and the centered
and uncentered conditional covariance estimates differ by

$$
\frac1n\sum_i z_i z_i^{\mathsf T}
-
\frac1n\sum_i\widetilde z_i\widetilde z_i^{\mathsf T}
=\bar z\bar z^{\mathsf T}=O_p(n^{-1}).
$$

The distinction is asymptotically negligible under the null but can matter in
small samples. Centering also makes explicit that the bootstrap reference is a
null reference while the observed numerator remains unchanged. The corrected
FIML procedure uses the observed-sensitivity effective rows without separate
within-pattern centering. The legacy API retains centering as a diagnostic.

### Studentization

Experiment 77 holds $V=G_A^{\mathsf T}IG_A$ fixed across multiplier draws. This
matches the multidimensional Hemerik--Goeman--Finos construction, which permits
a common convergent quadratic metric. It deliberately lets the resampling
distribution reproduce the weighted-chi-square spectrum induced by mismatch
between the sensitivity metric and the empirical score covariance.

A score-bootstrap variant may instead studentize the perturbed score with a
draw-specific covariance or "meat." One simple version defines

$$
\bar z_b^*=n^{-1}\sum_i\xi_{ib}z_i,
\qquad
\widehat B_b^*
=\sum_i
(\xi_{ib}z_i-\bar z_b^*)
(\xi_{ib}z_i-\bar z_b^*)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
T_b^{\mathrm{stud}}
=u_b^{\mathsf T}(\widehat B_b^*)^{-1}u_b.
$$

For Rademacher weights, the uncentered second-moment term is fixed because
$\xi_{ib}^2=1$; only the centering term varies. With Gaussian or Mammen weights,
the squared weights also change the meat. More elaborate score bootstraps may
evaluate the meat at a perturbed parameter. Studentization targets a more
pivotal statistic, but a draw-specific inverse can be unstable when $d$ is not
small relative to $n$ or the empirical meat is poorly conditioned. It is a
different calibration choice, not what makes a procedure a multiplier
bootstrap.

## The actual literature lineage

There are several converging lines, not one chain in which every later paper
cites every earlier paper.

1. **Score/LM testing.** @rao1948 introduced the score-test principle;
   @silvey1959 developed the constrained-likelihood Lagrange-multiplier
   formulation.
2. **Composite hypotheses and effective scores.** @neyman1959 and
   @hall_mathiason1990 supply the nuisance-orthogonal score construction.
   @boos1992 extends the score-test calculation to estimating equations and
   misspecified likelihoods using empirical variance estimates.
3. **Wild and weighted bootstrap.** @wu1986, @liu1988, @mammen1993, and
   @praestgaard_wellner1993 establish the broader idea of random weights that
   reproduce a heterogeneous empirical process.
4. **Estimating-function and score resampling.** @hu_zidek1995 and
   @hu_kalbfleisch2000 directly resample estimating-function summands.
   @kline_santos2012 explicitly perturbs M-estimator scores and proves results
   for LM and moment-restriction tests without refitting.
5. **Sign-flipped effective scores.** @hemerik_goeman_finos2020 combine
   Rademacher transformations, individual score contributions, effective-score
   nuisance correction, multidimensional quadratic statistics, and a
   permutation-style Monte Carlo rank. This is the closest constructional
   source for experiment 77.
6. **SEM moment geometry.** @shapiro1983 and @satorra1989 supply the saturated
   moment vector, model tangent, working metric, and weighted-chi-square
   asymptotics. Experiment 77 applies the score-multiplier construction to the
   local saturated complement under complete-data ML and observed-pattern FIML.

Hemerik, Goeman, and Finos frame their contribution through permutation and
sign-flip work, not through Kline--Santos or the classical wild-bootstrap
papers. Calling all these papers one explicit citation chain would therefore be
historically inaccurate. They are mathematically adjacent traditions that meet
at random weighting of casewise scores.

The Foldnes--Grønneberg--Moss pEBA work is not part of this lineage. It belongs
to the separate family that estimates or regularizes the eigenvalue spectrum of
the SEM quadratic-form limit.

## What may safely be claimed for experiment 77

The sources above support the construction and its first-order analogy. They do
not by themselves prove every feature of the FIML--SEM extension. A formal
validity argument still needs to state conditions ensuring:

- independent casewise observed-data scores, possibly non-identically
  distributed over missingness patterns;
- zero expected saturated score at the null pseudo-true moments;
- consistency of the working sensitivity $I$ used in the nuisance projection;
- a stable tangent rank and nonsingular $K^{\mathsf T}IK$ and
  $G^{\mathsf T}IG$;
- a Lindeberg condition and consistent empirical covariance for the projected
  rows;
- negligibility of replacing population moments, tangent, and information by
  their fitted versions; and
- an ignorable missingness argument appropriate to the claimed FIML setting.

In particular, the VM and independent-generator conditions used in experiment
77 do not generally make casewise scores exactly symmetric. MAR plus a working
Gaussian observed-data likelihood also requires more care than a correctly
specified parametric likelihood. The simulation can establish empirical
calibration in its design cells; it does not convert the procedure into an
exact finite-sample sign test.

Recommended wording is:

> We use Mammen multiplier calibration of observed-sensitivity
> nuisance-effective saturated scores. The realized observed-data Hessian
> removes the fitted SEM tangent, and the multipliers reproduce the conditional
> law of the resulting casewise score sum. The construction belongs to the
> estimating-function and score wild-bootstrap lineage. We retain the
> expected-information Rademacher version as an ablation, where each draw is
> algebraically a sign flip. Validity under the nonnormal FIML design is
> asymptotic rather than based on finite-sample sign invariance.
